definition.text: A change in environmental conditions that causes a marked change in an ecosystem.

facts.text: Disturbances include fires, floods, storms, insect outbreaks, trampling, earthquakes, plant diseases and volcanic eruptions.
They range in scale from a single tree falling to a mass extinction.
Many ecosystems are maintained by regular disturbance; wetlands, for example, by moving water and periodic fires.
Right after a disturbance there is a pulse of regrowth because competition for space and resources is low.
Biological diversity depends on natural disturbance; many shade-intolerant plants need it to establish.
In western US ponderosa pine forests, suppressing surface fires lets dense Douglas fir take over, cutting light, plant diversity and the animals that rely on them.
How species cope with disturbance may predict their ability to adapt to climate change.

definition.text: Disturbance to ecosystems caused by human activity.

facts.text: Logging, dredging, converting land to ranching or farming, mowing and mining are examples.
Human disturbance worldwide has spread disturbance-adapted species, often called weeds.
Controlled burns by Native Americans maintained fire-dependent ecosystems and helped keep them stable and diverse.
Human-caused climate change is considered a major force shaping future ecosystem change.

definition.text: Repeating patterns in which disturbance, regrowth and succession set an ecosystem up for the next disturbance.

facts.text: Without further disturbance, many ecosystems drift back toward pre-disturbance conditions through ecological succession.
Mountain pine beetle outbreaks in western North America kill old pines, opening gaps where other trees thrive until pines regrow.
In 2004 the beetles affected more than 90,000 square kilometres.

definition.text: Pioneer or early successional species that quickly exploit freshly disturbed sites.

facts.text: Fast-growing, shade-intolerant species such as pin cherry and aspen fill gaps left by fire or windstorms.
Jack pine has serotinous cones that open only with the heat of fire.

title: Ecological stability

definition.text: An ecosystem's ability to return to equilibrium after a disturbance, or to avoid sudden large changes over time.

facts.text: An ecosystem can be stable in some properties and not others; a plant community in drought may keep its biomass but lose biodiversity.
In 1997 Grimm and Wissel counted 167 definitions in the literature covering 70 different stability concepts.
They proposed replacing the term with more specific ones such as constancy, resilience and persistence.
Not every ecosystem is stable, as with wolves and moose on Isle Royale.
The concept emerged in the first half of the 20th century and spread with theoretical ecology in the 1970s.

contested_note: Overuse of the term has led to controversy over how ecological stability should be defined.

definition.text: The separate kinds of stability ecologists measure, such as constancy, resistance, persistence and resilience.

facts.text: Resistance measures how little a variable changes under outside pressure; inertia or persistence is the ability to resist fluctuations.
Resilience is the tendency to keep structure and recover after disturbance; elasticity is how fast it returns and amplitude how far it can be moved and still return.
Local stability covers small, short disturbances; global stability means strong resistance to change in species composition or food webs.

title: May stability criterion
article: Ecological stability#May stability analysis and random matrix theory

definition.text: Robert May's result that a large random ecosystem loses stability once its species number and interaction strength pass a limit.

facts.text: May linearised the species equations around equilibrium using the Jacobian, also called the community matrix.
Treating the Jacobian as a random matrix, the system loses stability when S exceeds 1/σ, where σ is the spread of interaction strengths.
The result implies diversity limits dynamical stability.

title: Diversity–stability debate

definition.text: The long-running question of whether more diverse ecosystems are more stable.

facts.text: Charles Elton argued in 1958 that complex, diverse communities tend to be more stable; Robert May later refuted the idea that diversity begets stability.
Diversity can stabilise ecosystem functions; genetic diversity, for example, can improve resistance to disturbance.
In food-web models the effect of diversity on stability can be positive or negative, depending on network structure.

contested_note: Elton held that diversity brings stability while May's models showed it can limit stability; evidence points both ways.
